sentences.text: Camarillasaurus was a medium-sized dinosaur reaching approximately 4 meters in length.
Its slender body was supported by fragmentary remains including a tooth, a possible neck vertebra, and parts of the rib cage and leg.
The species was first described in 2012 based on fossils found in the Camarillas Formation in Teruel Province, Spain.
New material recovered in 2018, including a femur and a foot bone, helped refine its classification.
Camarillasaurus was likely a bipedal predator with long hind legs.
The dinosaur is classified in the family Spinosauridae and the subfamily Spinosaurinae.
The type species of the genus is Camarillasaurus cirugedae.
A 2024 study placed it either as the basalmost spinosaurine or as a basal spinosaurid sister to Baryonychinae and Spinosaurinae.
However, in 2025, Rauhut and colleagues found high support for placing Camarillasaurus within Spinosaurinae as the sister taxon to a clade containing Spinosaurus and a Kem Kem spinosaurid.
This animal lived during the Barremian stage, from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago, in what is now northeastern Spain.

Since its initial description in 2012, Camarillasaurus was interpreted as a basal ceratosaur, serving as a key representative for understanding early diversity and evolution of this group in Laurasia during the Early Cretaceous.

Subsequent studies proposed including Camarillasaurus within the Spinosauridae, modifying its scientific relevance by integrating it into the context of spinosaurid radiation in Europe. In a 2019 EAVP conference summary, Oliver Rauhut and colleagues suggested it was instead a member of the Spinosauridae family rather than a ceratosaurian. A 2021 formal publication by Samathi supported the conclusion that Camarillasaurus is similar to Thai spinosaurid materials and other family taxa.

Due to fragmentary fossil material and differing phylogenetic interpretations, Camarillasaurus remains a reference taxon in debates regarding the evolution of European Early Cretaceous theropods and the presence and diversity of spinosaurids in Western Europe.
